title: The release map as project and stage plan
blurb: Describe the release map: what it shows, how it serves as the project and stage plan, and where it is created, approved and updated.
question: At the end of a stage, the project manager must give the board a plan for the next stage. In PRINCE2 Agile, what form does that plan take, and how detailed should it be?

teach.h: One visual plan for project and stage
teach.body: A release map is a visual plan showing how many releases the project expects, when each will happen and which features each will deliver. In PRINCE2 Agile it represents the project plan, and a stage plan is the same thing with a shorter horizon. Other plan elements, such as the budget, tolerances and assumptions, are included in the release map or referred to from it.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.4.4, 8.3.2.5 and Table 8.1

teach.h: A release map across two stages
teach.caption: Each release groups user stories from the story map and spans three iterations here; the usual range is two to four.

teach.body: The release map uses information from the story map. User stories are clustered into releases that make sense from a priority and a development or technical point of view, then the releases are visually separated and given deadlines. Releases usually contain two to four iterations. Iteration, release and stage are the three timebox levels PRINCE2 Agile names.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.2.5 and Glossary

teach.body: At a stage boundary the release map for the next stage is planned at a high level, in the release planning workshop. The next iterations can be outlined, but not broken into tasks yet: planning too early carries its own risks. The task-level plan for each iteration is made by the team in managing product delivery, when that iteration is about to start.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.2.5; Tables 13.15 and 13.16

teach.body: Thornbury is replacing paper slot bookings with an online portal. At the end of stage 1, project manager Aisha Mensah runs a release planning workshop with the product owners. They break key activities into user stories and update the release map: release 3 in iterations 7 to 9 now covers reporting and discounts. A board member asks for a task list for every iteration. Aisha explains that tasks are planned by the team each iteration, and submits the updated release map for approval.

teach.text: The release map is the plan; the story map is the breakdown that feeds it; the team plan holds the tasks for the next iteration. A stage plan in PRINCE2 Agile is not a separate detailed schedule: it is a release map with a shorter horizon. Do not confuse the release map with the project canvas (business case) or a burn chart (progress).

items: Release map: how many releases, when, and which features (8.4.4).
It represents the project plan; a stage plan is the same with a shorter horizon.
Budget, tolerances and assumptions are included or referred to.
Built from the story map; a release is usually two to four iterations.
Timebox levels: iteration, release and stage.
High level at stage boundaries; task-level plans for the next iteration only.

summary: You can now describe the release map as the PRINCE2 Agile form of the project and stage plan, built from the story map and kept high level. You can also say where it is documented, updated and approved across the processes.

A.q: Which PRINCE2 plans does the release map represent in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: The project plan and stage plan
The team plan and work package
The business case and project brief
The highlight and end stage reports
A.why: Release planning is incorporated into the plans: both the project plan and a stage plan are represented by a release map (8.4.4, Table 8.1).

whyNot.1: The team plan stays a team plan, and a work package description becomes a set of user stories.
whyNot.2: The business case becomes the project canvas; the project brief remains a brief.
whyNot.3: Highlight and end stage reports are replaced by the project dashboard.

A.q: How many iterations does a release usually contain?
options: One
Two to four
Five to seven
Eight to ten
A.why: Releases are given deadlines that usually contain two to four iterations (8.3.2.5).

whyNot.0: One iteration is the smallest timebox, not a typical release.
whyNot.2: Five to seven is longer than the usual release.
whyNot.3: Eight to ten would be several typical releases.

A.q: Which are the three timebox levels named in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Task, iteration and release
Sprint, epic and stage
Day, week and month
Iteration, release and stage
A.why: The glossary names three timebox levels: iteration, release and stage.

whyNot.0: A task is not a timebox level; stage is missing.
whyNot.1: Sprint is the Scrum word for iteration, and an epic is a large user story, not a timebox.
whyNot.2: Calendar periods are not the timebox levels the method names.

B.q: What should a release map clearly show?
options: Each team member's tasks for the iteration
How many releases, when, and which features
Who makes which decisions in each team
The status of each risk on the register
B.why: A release map shows how many releases are expected, when they will take place and what features each will release (8.4.4).

whyNot.0: Iteration tasks belong in the team plan.
whyNot.2: Decision authority is shown in the delegation matrix.
whyNot.3: Risk status is recorded in the risk register and shown on dashboards.

B.q:
Which two statements about the release map are correct?
1. It holds the task-level plan for every iteration in the stage.
2. A stage plan is a release map with a shorter horizon.
3. It replaces the project product description.
4. Budget, tolerances and assumptions are included or referred to.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Statements 2 and 4 match 8.4.4 and Table 8.1. Task plans sit in team plans, and the project backlog replaces the project product description.

whyNot.0: Statement 1 is false: task-level planning is done per iteration in team plans.
whyNot.1: Both are false: tasks are in team plans, and the project backlog replaces the project product description.
whyNot.3: Statement 3 is false: the project backlog, not the release map, replaces the project product description.

B.q: At a stage boundary, a project manager proposes a task-by-task plan for every iteration of the next stage. What does PRINCE2 Agile recommend instead?
options: A high-level release map, with tasks planned per iteration
A full Gantt chart of every task, approved by the board
A team plan covering the whole stage, agreed with the CPO
A story map for the stage, with no release dates set
B.why: At the boundary the release map is created at a high level; the team plans each iteration at task level in managing product delivery, avoiding the risks of planning too early (8.3.2.5).

whyNot.1: A task-level schedule for the whole stage is exactly the early detailed planning agile avoids.
whyNot.2: Team plans cover the next iteration and are produced by the team, not agreed by the CPO for a whole stage.
whyNot.3: The story map feeds the plan, but the plan needs releases with deadlines: the release map.

C.q: In which process, and which workshop, is the release map updated for the next stage?
options: Managing product delivery; team planning
Managing a stage boundary; release planning
Controlling a stage; progress review
Directing a project; agile enablement
C.why: Managing a stage boundary prepares the next stage plan by updating the release map, supported by the release planning workshop (Tables 13.15 and 13.16).

whyNot.0: Team planning produces the team plan for the next iteration, not the next stage.
whyNot.2: Progress reviews assess current status and demo products; next-stage planning is at the boundary.
whyNot.3: The agile enablement workshop reviews Agilometer results and agile-adoption risks.

C.q: In the 'directing a project' process, which activity approves the updated release map for the next stage, and what else does the board review?
options: Authorize initiation; the dashboards of each team
Give ongoing direction; the team plans for the next stage
Authorize the project; the story map and team plans
Authorize a stage or exception plan; the project dashboard
C.why: In 'authorize a stage or exception plan' the board reviews the updated project dashboard and approves the updated release map (Table 13.4).

whyNot.0: Authorize initiation approves the project brief and the release map for initiation; the board pulls from the project dashboard, not team dashboards.
whyNot.1: Ongoing direction is informal guidance; it is not where the next stage plan is approved.
whyNot.2: Authorizing the project approves the PID; the story map and team plans are planning inputs below board level.

C.q: How is a release map created, and which artifact supplies its input?
options: Tasks are scheduled by the PM; the team plan
Epics are costed by the board; the project canvas
Stories are clustered into releases; the story map
Risks are ranked by priority; the risk register
C.why: A release map is created from story-map information by clustering user stories into suitable releases (8.3.2.5).

whyNot.0: Task scheduling is the team's job for each iteration, and the team plan is not the input.
whyNot.1: The project canvas is the business case; it does not supply release content.
whyNot.3: Risks shape planning, but releases are built from user stories on the story map.

reteach.title: A timetable, not a minute-by-minute script
reteach.question: If you planned a three-month allotment season, would you write down every weed you will pull, or decide what to harvest each month and plan each weekend as it comes?

blocks.body: The release map is the season plan: which harvest (release) comes when, and what it contains. It serves as the project plan and, with a shorter horizon, the stage plan. The weekend jobs (tasks) are planned by the team each iteration.

blocks.text: Story map = breakdown. Release map = project and stage plan. Team plan = tasks for the next iteration.

explain.body: A visual plan of how many releases, when, and which features. It serves as the project plan and stage plan.

test.q: Which statement BEST describes a release map?
options: A chart of points left in an iteration
A visual plan of releases and features
A matrix of who decides what
A one-page business justification
test.why: A release map is a visual plan showing the releases, their timing and their features (8.3.2.5, 8.4.4).

whyNot.0: Points remaining in an iteration are shown on a burn-down chart.
whyNot.2: Who decides what is shown in a delegation matrix.
whyNot.3: A one-page business justification is the project canvas.

explain.body: PRINCE2 Agile names three timebox levels: iteration, release and stage. A release usually spans two to four iterations.

test.q: Which is NOT one of the three timebox levels in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Iteration
Release
Stage
Task
test.why: The three timebox levels are iteration, release and stage (Glossary). A task is a unit of work in a team plan.

explain.body: Release map for initiation in starting up; documented in initiation; updated during and at the end of each stage; final actuals at closure.

test.q: In which activity of 'initiating a project' is the release map documented?
options: Prepare the project plan
Agree tailoring requirements
Establish project controls
Prepare the full business case
test.why: In 'prepare the project plan' the PM, among other things, documents the release map (Table 13.6).

whyNot.1: Tailoring requirements are agreed and recorded in the PID.
whyNot.2: Project controls set stage boundaries, tolerances and escalation.
whyNot.3: The full business case is a more detailed project canvas.

explain.body: Plans are made just in time to avoid the risks of planning too early: high-level release map at boundaries, tasks per iteration.

test.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile avoid task-level planning far ahead?
options: The board approves each task directly
Velocity is fixed once initiation ends
To avoid the risks of planning too early
Tasks are set out in the project canvas
test.why: Plans are made just in time to avoid planning too early and its inherent risks (8.3.2.5).

whyNot.0: The board approves plans such as the release map, not individual tasks.
whyNot.1: Velocity is measured and refreshed as work continues, not fixed.
whyNot.3: The project canvas holds the business justification, not tasks.
